title: Magnetic noise of a dark exciton Bose-Einstein condensate
abstract: Excitons provide a promising platform for the realization of solid-state Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC), offering quantum coherence, strongly correlated electron-hole physics, and superfluidity. Yet, its unambiguous experimental identification remains challenging. In particular, $S_z= \pm 1$ triplet excitons are excellent candidates to realize an exciton BEC, because of their intrinsically limited recombination rate and thus long lifetimes. However, since their optical detection is inherently forbidden, experimental signatures remain elusive. In this work, we demonstrate that the magnetic nature of a $S_z= \pm 1$ triplet exciton BEC gives rise to stray magnetic field noise, that can be measured using nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center magnetometry. Using an external magnetic field to tune the system from an antiferromagnetic to a ferromagnetic ordering, the longitudinal spin sound mode of the BEC softens, bringing the mode into the characteristic gigahertz frequency range of the NV spin relaxation rate and thus allowing direct detection. Furthermore, we demonstrate an unconventional UV scaling at small distances $d$ from the sample, owing to the cubic corrections to the sound mode dispersion and damping rate in the form of Beliaev damping. Through this approach, we establish that the spin component of exciton BECs offers new approaches to detect exciton BECs.
summary: The authors propose using the stray magnetic field noise generated by an exciton Bose-Einstein Condensate as a novel detection method, circumventing the challenge of direct optical detection. By tuning the system's magnetic ordering near a critical point, they predict that the collective spin sound mode will soften into a measurable frequency range detectable by NV center magnetometry. This establishes a powerful link between condensed matter quantum phases and high-precision quantum sensing.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop a novel, measurable technique to experimentally detect exciton Bose-Einstein Condensates (BECs) formed by optically dark triplet excitons.
main_result: The magnetic nature of the BEC allows for the detection of collective spin sound modes via stray magnetic field noise measured using Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) center magnetometry, particularly near a quantum phase transition.
method: Theoretical calculations involving Bogoliubov theory and mean-field approximations are combined with predictions derived from the fluctuation-dissipation theorem applied to NV center magnetometry measurements.
model_or_system: The system is an exciton BEC composed of $S_z = \pm 1$ triplet excitons in a solid-state platform (like TMDs). The physics is governed by interactions and tuned via an external magnetic field, allowing tuning between antiferromagnetic and ferromagnetic ordering.
key_observables: Stray magnetic field noise measured by NV center magnetometry; the softening frequency of the longitudinal spin sound mode ($\omega_{-1}$); and unconventional UV scaling in the low-frequency $T_1^{-1}$ rate.
important_parameters: External magnetic field ($B$), critical field ($B_c$), spin polarization ($f_z$), and distance from the sample ($d$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes quasi-equilibrium for excitons, neglects static/thermal contributions to susceptibility in some parts, and relies on the NV center acting as a momentum filter.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematic magnetic noise measurements, the dependence of $T_1^{-1}$ on frequency near $B_c$, and numerically derived scaling laws for the low-frequency reduced transition rate versus distance $d$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical challenge (dark excitons) to developing a theoretical framework using mean-field theory and Bogoliubov analysis. It then calculates key diagnostics like magnetic susceptibility and damping mechanisms (Beliaev/Landau), culminating in relating these fluctuations to measurable NV center spin relaxation rates.
why_interesting: This work bridges the gap between highly correlated, solid-state quantum matter (exciton BECs) and advanced quantum sensing techniques (NV centers). The use of magnetic noise spectroscopy to probe collective excitations is a powerful methodology for studying otherwise inaccessible quantum phases.

NV sensing of materials.note: The core methodology involves using Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) center magnetometry to detect the stray magnetic field noise generated by a quantum system's collective excitations, which is central to NV sensing of magnetic properties.

Magnetic noise spectroscopy.note: The paper directly proposes using the measurement of 'stray magnetic field noise' from collective spin sound modes ($\omega_{-1}$) via fluctuation-dissipation theorems applied to NV center magnetometry, which is a direct extension of modeling magnetic noise near a probe.
